title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
description:
# Pacific Atlantic Water Flow

You are given an `m x n` matrix `heights` representing a rectangular island. The Pacific Ocean touches the island's top and left edges, and the Atlantic Ocean touches the island's bottom and right edges.

Water can flow from a cell to a 4-directionally adjacent cell if the neighboring cell's height is less than or equal to the current cell's height. A cell on an ocean border can flow directly into that ocean.

Return all coordinates `[r, c]` where water can flow from that cell to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans. The returned coordinates may be in any order.

Water may reach the two oceans along different paths from the same cell. A single path need not visit both oceans.

## Example 1

**Input:** `heights = [[1,2,2,3,5],[3,2,3,4,4],[2,4,5,3,1],[6,7,1,4,5],[5,1,1,2,4]]`

**Output:** `[[0,4],[1,3],[1,4],[2,2],[3,0],[3,1],[4,0]]`

**Explanation:** These cells can reach both oceans by following non-increasing height paths. For example, `(2, 2)` has height `5`, so it can flow toward the Pacific through the upper-left side and toward the Atlantic through the lower-right side.

## Example 2

**Input:** `heights = [[1]]`

**Output:** `[[0,0]]`

**Explanation:** The only cell touches all four borders, so it reaches both oceans.

## Constraints

* `m == heights.length`.
* `n == heights[r].length`.
* `1 <= m, n <= 200`.
* `0 <= heights[r][c] <= 100000`.

solutions.name: Reverse DFS from Ocean Borders
solutions.description:
## Approach
Run one DFS from all Pacific border cells and one DFS from all Atlantic border cells. In the reversed search, move only to neighbors whose height is greater than or equal to the current cell. A cell included in both visited sets is part of the answer.

## Key Insight
Forward water flow moves downhill or level. Reversing that direction turns each ocean's reachable region into an uphill-or-level flood fill from its border. This avoids starting a separate search from every cell.

## Complexity Analysis
Each ocean search visits each cell at most once. The time complexity is `O(m * n)`, and the visited arrays plus recursion stack use `O(m * n)` space.

solutions.name: Reverse BFS from Ocean Borders
solutions.description:
## Approach
Build two queues: one seeded with every Pacific border cell and one seeded with every Atlantic border cell. Each queue performs the same reverse-flow traversal, marking neighbors that are at least as high as the current cell.

## Key Insight
BFS and DFS mark the same reverse-reachable sets. The queue version makes the multi-source nature more explicit: all cells on an ocean border are starting points for that ocean at the same time.

## Complexity Analysis
Each cell can be enqueued once per ocean. The time complexity is `O(m * n)`, and the queues and visited arrays use `O(m * n)` space.

solutions.name: Combined Bitmask Queue Propagation
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use one integer mask per cell: bit `1` means Pacific-reachable, and bit `2` means Atlantic-reachable. Seed border cells with their ocean bits and enqueue a cell whenever it gains a new bit. Propagate that bit uphill or level to neighbors.

## Key Insight
The two ocean searches are the same data-flow problem. A single queue can propagate ocean reachability bits until no cell gains new information; cells with mask `3` can reach both oceans.

## Complexity Analysis
Each cell can gain each ocean bit once, so there are at most `2 * m * n` meaningful enqueues. Time and space are both `O(m * n)`.

solutions.name: Fixed-Point Reachability Propagation
solutions.timeComplexity: O((m * n)^2) in the worst case
solutions.description:
## Approach
Give each cell an ocean reachability mask based on whether it touches the Pacific or Atlantic border. Repeatedly scan the whole grid; a cell can inherit an ocean bit from any lower-or-equal neighbor because water can flow from the cell to that neighbor. Stop when a full pass makes no changes.

## Key Insight
This is a Bellman-Ford style fixed-point formulation. It is slower than border DFS or BFS, but it states the reachability rule directly: ocean bits move opposite the water-flow direction until no cell can improve.

## Complexity Analysis
Each scan costs `O(m * n)`, and the number of passes can be proportional to the number of cells in the worst case. The reachability table uses `O(m * n)` space.

tests.description: Canonical height map with seven cells that can reach both oceans.
Flat grid lets every cell flow to every border.
A single row touches both the top Pacific edge and bottom Atlantic edge.
A single column touches both the left Pacific edge and right Atlantic edge.
A central peak and ridge cells can drain to both oceans, while opposite low corners cannot.
A low center basin cannot climb to the ocean ring.
A descending southeast slope leaves only the Pacific border paths able to reach both oceans.
